---
subtitle: "How AI coding assistants may and may not be used in NCC work"
---

# AI tools {#sec-ai-tools}

AI coding assistants — Claude, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT and
similar — are useful for writing and reviewing analysis code, drafting
documentation, and explaining unfamiliar code. They are also a route by which
sensitive data can leave a protected environment, because everything typed into
a hosted assistant is sent to a third party. This page sets out how the study
group uses them.

::: {.callout-note}

## Who and what this applies to

This guidance applies to everyone doing NCC work — analysts, students,
collaborators — and to any AI assistant, whether it is a chat interface, an
editor plugin, or a command-line agent. It covers assistant use for analysis
code, documentation, and manuscript text.

It does **not** change any existing rule about data handling. Where this page
and the study's approvals or data processing agreements differ, the approvals
govern.

## The hard line

::: {.callout-important}
## Person-level NCC data must never be given to an AI assistant

NCC data is highly sensitive person-level health and registry data. It lives on
**TSD** and it does not leave TSD. Pasting it into a hosted assistant sends it
to a third party outside the study's approvals, and that is a personal-data
breach regardless of the assistant, the account, or the intention.

This applies to every form the data can take: rows from a dataset, a printout
of the first few records, a screenshot of the data viewer, identifiers, dates
of birth, free-text questionnaire answers, and small or raw cell counts —
including "just a couple of example rows" to illustrate a problem.
:::

There is no exception for a small excerpt, a de-identified-looking extract, an
assistant that claims not to train on inputs, or an enterprise account. If you
are unsure whether something counts, treat it as data and do not share it.

## Why TSD changes how assistants are used

TSD has **no internet access**, so no AI assistant runs inside TSD. Every
assistant you use is necessarily outside the secure environment. That gives the
working model the study already uses for analysis, applied to assistants:

1. **Code out.** You describe the problem to the assistant *outside* TSD, using
   code and structure only, and it writes or reviews code.
2. **Carry it in.** You copy the code into TSD by hand.
3. **Run it there.** The code executes against the real data inside TSD. The
   assistant is not involved in this step and cannot be.
4. **Sanitized results out.** You bring back only what is safe to bring back
   (see below) — typically an error message, a structural diagnostic, or an
   aggregated, suppression-checked result.

Two consequences are worth stating plainly. The assistant **has never seen your
data and cannot run your code**, so any claim it makes about what the code
produces is a prediction, not a result. And because each round trip costs real
manual effort, it is worth getting the code reviewed carefully before you carry
it across.

## What may and may not be shared

| Safe to share with an assistant | Never share with an assistant |
|---|---|
| Code — R scripts, do-files, Quarto documents | Any rows of real data, however few |
| Error messages and warnings, with data values removed | Identifiers, names, dates of birth, addresses |
| Variable **structure**: names, types, factor levels and labels, *without values* | Console output that prints real records |
| Cohort-level dimensions (row and column counts) | Small or raw cell counts below the suppression threshold |
| Aggregated results that already meet the study's disclosure rules | Free-text questionnaire answers |
| Dummy or synthetic data and its output | Screenshots of the data viewer or of raw output |
| Study documentation that is already public | Credentials, internal server names, or paths |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Ask for structure, not values

Most of the time an assistant does not need your data to help — it needs the
*shape* of your data. Variable names, types, and factor levels are enough to
write a correct join or a correct recode. If an assistant asks you for example
rows, give it the schema instead, or generate dummy data (below).
:::

- **Variable names and structure** — treated as shareable above, on the basis

- **Codebooks** — including full factor level and value labels. These can

- **Aggregate results** — decide whether results that already pass the study's

  derived from the real data goes to an assistant regardless of aggregation.

## Developing on dummy data

The reliable way to use an assistant well is to give it something it can
legitimately see: a **synthetic dataset that mirrors the real schema** — the
same variable names, types, and value labels, with entirely invented values.

- Generate dummy data from scratch. It must never be sampled, perturbed, or
  reconstructed from real records — a perturbed extract is still personal data.
- Label it unmistakably as synthetic, for example with a `dummy_` prefix and a
  header comment, so it can never be mistaken for a real extract.
- Set the study's agreed seed once, so the dummy data is reproducible.

Code developed and debugged against dummy data transfers cleanly into TSD, and
most errors are caught before they cost an air-gap round trip.

```r
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(936)

dummy_baseline <- tibble(
  deltaker_id = seq_len(500),
  B_Age_gr    = sample(c("18-39", "40-59", "60+"), 500, replace = TRUE),
  B_Sex       = sample(c("Female", "Male"), 500, replace = TRUE)
)
```

## Verification expectations

::: {.callout-warning}
## AI-written code is a draft until a human has read it

An assistant produces plausible code, not verified code. It cannot run against
NCC data, and it will state confidently that code works when it has never been
executed.
:::

Before AI-assisted code is used on real data:

1. **Read it line by line.** You are responsible for code you run on NCC data,
   whoever or whatever wrote it. If you cannot explain what a line does, do not
   run it.
2. **Check every variable name against the codebook.** Assistants working from
   a described schema will invent plausible variable names that do not exist,
   or use a name from a different questionnaire family.
3. **Check joins specifically.** Every NCC join is a `1:1` merge on
   `deltaker_id`; a join that changes the row count means something is wrong.
   Assert the expected row count in the code rather than checking by eye.
4. **Check that disclosure control survived.** If the code produces a table
   that will come out of TSD, confirm small-cell suppression is actually
   applied before anything is exported or screenshotted.

And for anything that reaches a manuscript:

::: {.callout-important}
No AI-generated result, table, figure, or number goes into a manuscript,
report, or presentation without a human having verified it against the analysis
output it claims to come from. The same applies to AI-drafted text making
factual claims about the study — check it against this manual.
:::

## TODO — study team: when AI assistance must be declared

Decide and record:

- **In publications** — which journal and funder AI-disclosure policies the
  group follows, what level of assistance triggers a declaration (code help
  versus drafted text versus generated analysis), and the wording to use. Note
  that most publishers require that AI tools are **not** listed as authors.
- **In internal analysis documentation** — whether analysis plans and analysis
  scripts should record that an assistant was used, and if so where (a header
  comment, a section in the plan, or a project log).
- **In this repository** — whether AI-assisted contributions to the
  documentation should be flagged in the pull request.
:::

Record who to ask before adopting a tool that is not on the list, and note that

that indexes a whole project directory or runs commands automatically needs
particular scrutiny, since it can read more than the user intends to share.
:::

## If data reaches an assistant anyway

If you realise that person-level data, identifiers, or an unsuppressed result
has been pasted into an assistant, treat it as a suspected personal-data breach
and report it immediately. Do not wait to establish how serious it was, and do
not try to resolve it by deleting the conversation — deletion does not undo the
transfer, and it destroys the record needed to assess what happened.
